tip: Hindi puts is/are at the very end: है (hai) or हैं (hain). मेरी बहन डॉक्टर है (meri bahan doctor hai) – literally 'my sister doctor is'.
है / हैं / हूँ / हो (hai / hain / hun / ho) normally sit at the end of the sentence. Not in the middle like English is/are.
Question words sit in the answer's slot: in कैसे हो (kaise ho = how are you), कैसे (kaise) fills the spot the answer ठीक (theek = fine) would take – no flipping to the front like English.
Never drop है/हैं/हूँ. मैं डॉक्टर is not a sentence – you need मैं डॉक्टर हूँ (main doctor hun = I am a doctor).
Possessives match the thing owned, not the owner: तुम्हारे बच्चे (tumhare bachche = your children) – तुम्हारे (tumhare) is plural because बच्चे is, whoever you are.
Hunger strikes you in Hindi: भूख लगी है (bhookh lagi hai = hunger has struck). Thirst and cold too: प्यास लगी है (pyaas lagi hai). You're the target, not the doer.
The verb ending shows the speaker's own gender: a man says पीता हूँ (peeta hun = I drink), a woman says पीती हूँ (peeti hun). Same I, different ending.
जी (ji) glued to a name or relative adds respect: चाचाजी (chachaji = uncle-ji). You'll hear it everywhere – पापाजी (papaji), even हाँ जी (haan ji) for a polite yes.
Present habit ends -ता/-ती/-ते by gender: माँ बनाती है (maa banaati hai = mom makes-f).
For polite आप or plural, use -ते: आप क्या करते हैं? (aap kya karte hain = What do you do?). Plural ending also signals respect.
पसंद आया (pasand aaya = liking came) is one-time – they liked it that day. For a standing taste, Hindi switches to पसंद है (pasand hai).
No word for 'than' – Hindi uses से (se = from): चीनी से ज़्यादा (chini se zyada = from sugar more) means 'more than sugar'.
Love is something you do in Hindi: प्यार करते हैं (pyaar karte hain = do love). And the loved one takes से: मुझसे (mujhse = literally 'from me').
Hindi chains actions with -कर (-kar = having done): नहाकर (nahakar = having bathed) means 'after bathing' – no 'and' needed between bathing and getting ready.
English 'takes time' flips in Hindi: समय लगता है (samay lagta hai = time attaches). The time attaches to the task – the task doesn't take it.
English drops 'then' but Hindi keeps it: अगर (agar = if) pairs with तो (to = then). Skipping the तो sounds unfinished to Hindi ears.
दौड़ता है (daudta hai) = runs, as a routine – not 'is running'. Right-now actions use रहा है (raha hai); the -ता (-ta) form is for habits.
There's no verb 'brush' here – Hindi makes teeth clean: दाँत साफ़ करता हूँ (daant saaf karta hoon). साफ़ (saaf = clean) + करना (karna = do) does the job.
English 'tells' the truth – Hindi speaks it: सच बोलता है (sach bolta hai). Truth and lies both pair with बोलना (bolna = speak), and there's no 'the'.
ये गाड़ियाँ चलती हैं (chalti hain) – literally 'walk'. चलना (chalna) is the verb for machines moving or working: cars, phones and fans all चलते (chalte).
Doubling a word tightens its meaning: सुबह (subah) = morning, सुबह-सुबह (subah-subah) = early in the morning, right at daybreak.
One grandmother, plural verb: दादी जाती हैं (daadi jaati hain), not है (hai). Elders take plural forms as respect – singular would sound rude.
'Studies' is noun + do: पढ़ाई करती है (padhaai karti hai = does studying). Hindi builds many verbs this way – काम करना (kaam karna = to work).
-कर (-kar) chains actions: स्कूल से आकर (school se aakar = having come from school). One small ending replaces the whole phrase 'after coming'.
You arrive 'on' work: काम पर (kaam par) पहुँचता है. पर is literally 'on', but it's the standard word for being at or heading to work.
भी (bhi = also) sits right after the word it highlights: तुम्हारी बहन भी (tumhaari bahan bhi) = your sister too. Move भी and the emphasis moves with it.
Hindi pairs opposites with a hyphen and skips 'and': दिन-रात (din-raat = day and night). Same pattern in माता-पिता (maata-pita = parents).
वाली (vaali) tags what something comes with: अदरक वाली चाय (adrak vaali chai) = ginger tea, roughly 'the ginger one'. Masculine nouns take वाला (vaala).
'Twice a day' is 'in a day two times': दिन में दो बार (din mein do baar). Everyday Hindi skips 'per' – में (mein = in) plus the time span covers it.
English shops just 'close' – Hindi shops become closed: बंद होती है (band hoti hai = gets closed). A person closing it would be बंद करना (band karna).
